text: What if no European ship had ever crossed the Atlantic? The Americas keep developing on their own terms — empires rising, cities growing, trade routes humming — and Europe stays small, poor, and hungry. [pause:0.75] That almost happened. Instead, three worlds collided — and nothing on this planet stayed the same. You're watching APUSH Explained. Let's get into it.

First, the setup. It's 1491. In the Americas, millions of people live in societies utterly different from one another. The Mexica run a tribute empire from Tenochtitlan, a city bigger than London. The Inca administer millions of subjects across the Andes. Mississippian farming towns dot the river valleys of the Southeast — the great mound city of Cahokia already risen and faded. In the Southwest, Pueblo peoples farm the desert; in the Pacific Northwest, fishing villages harvest the richest waters on earth.

Three worlds, remember — the Americas, Europe, and Africa — each running on its own logic. The Americas run on tribute and kinship. Europe runs on crusade and crown. Africa runs on gold and trade. [pause:0.45] The point is: none of them is waiting to be discovered. They're all busy being themselves.

First: why were some Native societies huge and hierarchical while others stayed small and mobile? The answer is one plant: maize. Where maize farming took hold, populations exploded, and dense populations needed organization — chiefs, priests, tribute systems. The Mexica built an empire on it. The Inca, high in the Andes, ran a command economy on maize and potatoes that fed millions without money or markets.

Where maize couldn't grow, life stayed smaller and more mobile — Pueblo farmers in the desert Southwest, fishing peoples in the Pacific Northwest, hunters on the Great Plains. [TIP]Remember this: agriculture, then population density, then social complexity — that chain explains almost every Native society you'll meet on this exam.[/TIP]

Second world: Europe. In 1491, Iberia is finishing an 800-year war — the Reconquista. When Granada falls, Spain will be newly unified, deeply Catholic, and spoiled for a fight. Portugal, next door, has spent decades perfecting the caravel — a ship that can sail into the Atlantic wind and come home again.

Third world: Africa. The Songhai Empire controls the trans-Saharan gold trade. The kingdom of Kongo thrives on the Atlantic coast. African kingdoms have traded with Europe for centuries — gold, salt, and, increasingly, enslaved people to work Portugal's new sugar plantations. [pause:0.45] The point is: when contact comes, it won't be strangers meeting. It'll be three old, confident worlds, each with its own reasons to want more.

And then, the collision. October 1492. Columbus isn't looking for a new world — he's hunting Asia, and he's lost by about eight thousand miles. Listen to how he describes the Taíno people who greet him, in his own journal:

quote.source: Christopher Columbus, journal of the first voyage (Las Casas abstract), entry of 13 October 1492

text: “They are very well built, with very handsome bodies and very good faces.”

Warm words. [pause:0.45] Now hear what comes two sentences later in the same journal — he notes they would make good servants, and he seizes several by force to carry back to Spain. [pause:0.75] The point is: curiosity and conquest arrive on the same ship. That pattern — wonder first, chains second — will repeat for the next three hundred years.

The catastrophe to come has a face, and it's in this book. The Florentine Codex, compiled by the friar Sahagún from Nahua witnesses, shows smallpox tearing through Tenochtitlan in 1520. The sick couldn't move; the healthy were too few to bury the dead.

Europeans called the Americas a virgin land. It wasn't virgin — it was emptied. Disease killed up to ninety percent of Native peoples, and every empire Spain built afterward was built on that silence. Remember this: the exchange went both ways, but the dying went mostly one way.
The Spanish who followed Columbus didn't see themselves as destroyers. Listen to Bernal Díaz, a foot soldier who marched with Cortés into Tenochtitlan, remembering what he saw:

quote.source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España

text: “Things never heard of, seen or dreamed of before.”

He means it as awe — a city of 200,000 rising from a lake, with markets, causeways, and aqueducts. The Spanish were genuinely stunned. [pause:0.45] And they tore it down anyway, stone by stone, and built Mexico City on the rubble. Awe didn't save Tenochtitlan. Nothing did.
Cortés himself, writing to the king of Spain to justify the conquest, brags about the great market at Tlatelolco:

quote.source: Hernán Cortés, Second Letter to Charles V

text: “Where there are daily assembled more than sixty thousand souls.”

Sixty thousand souls, buying and selling every day — a market bigger than Seville. [pause:0.75] He describes it in loving detail — and then claims it all for Spain. The point is: the Spanish knew exactly what they were taking. This wasn't an accident of history. It was a robbery the robbers wrote down.

So the point is this. Three worlds, three logics — tribute empires, crusading kingdoms, trading states — smashed into each other, and the result rewired the planet. Europe got the potato, maize, the tomato. The Americas got wheat, horses, sugar — and smallpox. [pause:0.75] Historians call it the Columbian Exchange. Hold onto this: it was never equal. Europe was changed; the Americas were transformed — and their peoples paid for it with their lives. Three worlds went in. One world system came out.

That's the world in 1491 — three worlds on the eve of the collision. Next, we zoom in on Native America itself: why maize made empires, and how a dozen different societies adapted to a continent. That's vid-u1-02, plus the drill set at the link. Drill it, own it — I'll see you in the next one.
